intro: A gym shirt dries on the shower rod in two hours while the jeans beside it are still wet in the morning. A wool sweater comes out of a hot wash small enough for a child. A shiny blouse snags on a ring the first day. None of this is luck. Every piece of clothing behaves the way its fiber, its yarn and its fabric construction tell it to, and all three are written on a tag most people never read. This unit teaches you to read the tag, feel the fabric and know what will happen before it happens.

The first chapter is textile science. You will learn the four common natural fibers and the four common manufactured ones, what each one does well and badly, how yarns become woven or knit fabric, and what the plain, twill and satin weaves look like from across a room. You will learn the five care symbols that let you wash anything, read the standard burn-test results without ever striking a match, and put numbers on what fast fashion costs beyond the price on the tag.

The second chapter is pattern work. You will decode a pattern envelope, measure a body and pick a size from the chart instead of a store label, find the selvage, the grain and the bias on a bolt of fabric, lay out pieces on grain, cut and mark them, and understand why a pattern is bigger than the body on purpose. Then you will change the length of a piece on paper, sew a test garment, and carry every fit fix back to the tissue. By the end, a length of fabric and a paper envelope will look like a garment you know how to make.
bigQuestion: How do you read a fabric and a pattern well enough to know, before you cut, how a garment will feel, fit, wash and last?

timeline.t: Eli Whitney's cotton gin makes cleaning cotton fiber fast and cotton cloth cheap
Jacquard's punched-card loom weaves complex patterns automatically
Butterick begins selling graded paper patterns in standard sizes
Rayon, the first manufactured fiber, is developed from wood cellulose
Nylon, the first fully synthetic fiber, is invented at DuPont
Polyester fiber is patented in England; it becomes the world's most used fiber
Spandex is developed, bringing stretch to blended fabrics
The Textile Fiber Products Identification Act takes effect, requiring fiber content on tags
The FTC Care Labeling Rule takes effect; U.S. garments must carry care instructions
Standard care symbols are allowed in place of words on U.S. care labels

words.d: the smallest hair-like strand that yarn and fabric are made from
the plant material that cotton, linen and rayon fibers are made of
a fiber from an animal, such as wool or silk
a fiber made in a factory, such as polyester, nylon, rayon or spandex
fabric made of yarns crossing at right angles; stable, crisp, frays when cut
fabric made of yarn loops; stretches, resists wrinkles, needs a stretch stitch
a weave with a diagonal line on the surface, as in denim; tough and dirt-hiding
the washtub, triangle, square, iron and circle marks that show how to launder a garment
the finished long edge of a woven fabric; the lengthwise grain runs parallel to it
the diagonal of a woven fabric, stretchiest at 45 degrees to the grain
the double-headed arrow on a pattern piece that must lie parallel to the selvage
the room between a body measurement and the finished garment at the same place

test.q: Which fiber is a hollow tube of cellulose that soaks up water?
test.why: Cotton fibers are hollow cellulose tubes, which is why cotton absorbs and holds water.

test.q: A wool sweater felts in the wash. What combination caused it?
test.why: Heat and agitation lock the scales on wool fibers together, shrinking the fabric permanently.

test.q: Why does an iron on the cotton setting damage a polyester shirt?
choices: Polyester absorbs the steam and swells
Polyester is plastic and melts at that heat
test.why: Polyester is a petroleum-based plastic fiber that melts and glazes at cotton-setting temperatures.

test.q: Which fiber starts as wood pulp but is shaped in a factory?
test.why: Rayon is regenerated cellulose, made by dissolving wood pulp and forcing it through a spinneret.

test.q: On a U.S. clothing tag, what does federal law require about fiber content?
choices: Each fiber listed by percentage, largest first
test.why: The Textile Fiber Products Identification Act requires every fiber by percentage in descending order.

test.q: A cut fabric edge frays as loose yarns slip out. What kind of fabric is it?
test.why: Woven fabrics fray at cut edges; knit edges curl or run instead.

test.q: Which weave has long floating yarns that make it shiny and easy to snag?
test.why: In a satin weave a yarn floats over four or more yarns, reflecting light and catching on rough surfaces.

test.q: A care tag shows a triangle with diagonal lines inside. What does it mean?
test.why: The triangle is bleach; diagonal lines inside mean non-chlorine (color-safe) bleach only.

test.q: In the standard burn-test description, which fiber group melts into a hard bead?
choices: Plastic fibers such as polyester and nylon
test.why: Polyester and nylon melt and cool into a hard bead; cotton leaves ash and wool a crushable black bead.

test.q: Why does a pattern size often differ from a store size?
choices: Store sizes are measured in centimeters
Pattern companies use their own body-measurement charts
Patterns run one size small on purpose
Store sizes include ease and patterns do not
test.why: Pattern sizing follows the chart on the envelope, which is separate from ready-to-wear sizing; measure and use the chart.

test.q: How do you confirm a pattern piece is on grain?
choices: Match its notches to the selvage
Fold it in half and compare
Measure from both ends of the grainline arrow to the selvage until equal
test.why: Equal distances from each arrowhead to the selvage put the grainline parallel to the lengthwise grain.

test.q: Which direction of a woven fabric should bias tape be cut on, and why?
choices: The selvage, so it does not fray
True bias, so it stretches around curves without puckering
test.why: Bias-cut strips give and shape around necklines and armholes; grain-cut strips fight the curve.

test.q: What happens if you unpin the tissue before marking dots and darts?
choices: The positions of the dots and darts are lost
test.why: Marks are transferred while the tissue is pinned; afterward there is no way to find where the darts were.

test.q: To shorten a bodice by 1 inch at the lengthen-or-shorten line, how deep a tuck do you fold?
test.why: A folded tuck removes twice its depth, so a ½-inch tuck removes 1 inch.

test.q: Tight diagonal lines on a test garment point toward the armholes. What do they show?
choices: The garment is too tight there
The piece was cut on the bias
test.why: Pulling lines point to the spot where a garment is too small; loose folds mean too much fabric.

write.prompt: Choose a simple garment (a drawstring bag, a pillowcase or a sleeveless top) and write a start-to-finish plan: the fiber and fabric you would choose and why, the size and yardage you would buy, and the steps from preshrinking through layout, cutting, marking and one fit check. Explain why each step is there and what would go wrong without it.
tips: Name the fiber and the construction (woven or knit) and connect each to a property the garment needs.
Put the steps in order: preshrink, straighten grain, fold, lay out on grain, pin, cut, mark, unpin.
Give the real numbers: fabric width, yardage, the 5/8-inch seam allowance, the pin spacing, the tuck depth if you adjust length.
For every step, write one sentence on the mistake it prevents.
End with how the care label for your fabric will read, symbol by symbol.
